# Le Café des Questions

*The Café of Questions*

A 20-episode story in a tiny Montmartre café whose owner serves you only after one question. In a tiny café on a steep street in Montmartre, Madame Rose, 70, has one rule, chalked on the slate by the door and signed O.: one question, then a coffee. Each customer walks in with a problem, and her simple question helps them see it differently, while Socrate, her grumpy grey parrot, gives his opinion without a word. Episode by episode, small clues show why she made the rule.

## How to read

Each line gives the speaker and the French, then the English in italics. The respellings (English-style pronunciation, not IPA) are only in the word list at the end of each episode; **‿** marks a liaison there (*vous avez* = voo‿zah-vay). The questions for every episode and the answer key are at the end. The word in brackets after the English, such as *(teasing)*, says how the line is said.

### Pronunciation key

| Spelling | Sounds like |
|---|---|
| **zh** | the "s" in *measure* (French **j** / soft **g**) |
| **uh** | the "a" in *about* |
| **ew** | French **u**: say "ee" with your lips rounded like "oo" |
| **N** (capital) | nasal vowel: hum the vowel through your nose, don't say the "n" |
| **ahN** | nasal *an / en* (as in *France*) |
| **ohN** | nasal *on* (as in *bon*) |
| **aN** | nasal *in / ain / ien* (as in *vin*) |
| **uhN** | nasal *un* (as in *un*) |
| **r** | French throaty "r", made at the back of the throat |
| **‿** | liaison: the silent final consonant is pronounced at the start of the next word (*vous‿avez* = voo zah-vay) |

Tips: final consonants are usually silent (*parlent* = "parl"). A hyphen joins syllables said as one word; a liaison consonant is written at the start of the next syllable (*les amis* = lay zah-mee).

## Act 1 · Une question, puis un café (One question, then a coffee)

*Level A1*

### Episode 1 · La règle (The rule)

*On Monday at half past eight, Thomas rushes into a tiny café in Montmartre with a phone in each hand. Madame Rose puts a white cup on her side of the counter and taps the slate by the door, signed O. When a phone rings, Thomas answers it, and Socrate, the grey parrot by the window, turns his back on him. Later Thomas puts both phones down, and Rose slides the cup across.*

**Thomas:** Bonjour ! Un café, vite ! Je suis en retard.
> *Morning! A coffee, quick! I'm late.* (worried)

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. Vite ? Ici, une question, puis un café.
> *Good morning. Quick? Here, it's one question, then a coffee.* (teasing)

**Thomas:** Une question ? Pour un café ? Je n'ai pas le temps !
> *A question? For a coffee? I haven't got time! (US: I don't have time)* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Socrate vous tourne le dos. Il n'est pas d'accord.
> *Socrate's turning his back on you. He doesn't approve.* (amused)

**Thomas:** Pardon. Et sur l'ardoise, c'est qui, O. ?
> *Sorry. And on the slate, who's O.?* (curious)

**Rose:** Ici, c'est moi qui pose les questions.
> *Here, I'm the one who asks the questions.* (teasing)

**Rose:** Qu'est-ce que vous aimez, le matin ?
> *What do you like, in the morning?* (curious)

**Thomas:** Le matin ? Je cours. Je travaille. Avec mon café.
> *In the morning? I rush around. I work. Coffee in hand.* (worried)

**Thomas:** J'aime… le café. Et le silence.
> *I like… coffee. And silence.* (surprised)

**Thomas:** Merci. Je m'assois. Je reste cinq minutes.
> *Thanks. I'll sit down. I'll stay five minutes.* (relieved)

#### Words from this episode

- **Je suis en retard** (zhuh swee‿zahN ruh-tar) — I'm late
- **un café** (uhN kah-fay) — a coffee (un: masculine)
- **Je n'ai pas le temps** (zhuh nay pah luh tahN) — I haven't got time (US: I don't have time)
- **pas d'accord** (pah dah-kor) — doesn't agree (d'accord: OK, agreed)
- **c'est moi qui pose les questions** (seh mwah kee pohz lay kes-tyohN) — I'm the one who asks the questions (poser une question: to ask a question)
- **Qu'est-ce que vous aimez** (kes-kuh voo‿zeh-may) — What do you like
- **Je cours** (zhuh koor) — I run, I rush around (courir)
- **Je travaille** (zhuh trah-vahy) — I work (je: -e; vous travaillez)
- **Je reste cinq minutes** (zhuh rest saNk mee-newt) — I'll stay five minutes (present for a decision now)

#### Notice: Present-tense endings: vous aimez, j'aime

Rose asks Qu'est-ce que vous aimez, le matin ? and Thomas answers J'aime… le café. The stem aim- stays the same; only the ending changes: -ez for vous, -e for je. Thomas's Je travaille works the same way: vous travaillez. See the table: Grammar tables, Present-tense endings.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Chaque chose en son temps. »** (shahk shohz ahN sohN tahN)

*Literally:* Each thing in its time.

*Meaning:* Give each thing its own moment: finish your coffee before the next task.

*English equivalent:* All in good time.

### Episode 2 · Le discours (The speech)

*On Thursday Paul sits at one of Madame Rose's three little tables with twelve pages and a pen: on Saturday he marries Léa. Rose drinks from her own blue cup with an O painted on it; customers get white ones. She puts Paul's white cup on her side of the counter. Later Socrate, the grey parrot, nibbles page twelve.*

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. Un thé ? Vous êtes tout blanc.
> *Hello. A tea? You're as white as a sheet. (literally: all white)* (curious)

**Paul:** Samedi, je me marie. Écoutez : l'amour est une étoile…
> *I'm getting married on Saturday. Listen: 'Love is a star…'* (worried)

**Rose:** Douze pages ? Pour un mariage ?
> *Twelve pages? For a wedding?* (amused)

**Paul:** Je sais. J'écris, j'écris… et j'ai peur.
> *I know. I write and write… and I'm scared.* (worried)

**Rose:** Votre thé, après une question. La règle a quarante ans.
> *Your tea comes after one question. The rule is forty years old.* (teasing)

**Rose:** Pourquoi vous aimez Léa ?
> *Why do you love Léa?* (curious)

**Paul:** Parce qu'elle rit tout le temps. Parce qu'elle est gentille.
> *Because she laughs all the time. Because she's kind.* (moved)

**Paul:** Parce qu'avec elle, je suis moi.
> *Because with her, I'm me.* (proud)

**Rose:** Voilà votre discours. Et voilà votre thé.
> *There's your speech. And here's your tea.* (proud)

**Paul:** Ouf ! Et Socrate mange la page douze. Onze pages, alors !
> *Phew! And Socrate's eating page twelve. Eleven pages, then!* (amused)

**Rose:** Non, monsieur. Trois phrases. C'est tout.
> *No. Three sentences. That's all.* (teasing)

#### Words from this episode

- **Vous êtes tout blanc** (voo‿zet too blahN) — You're as white as a sheet (être: vous êtes)
- **je me marie** (zhuh muh mah-ree) — I'm getting married (se marier: me for je)
- **Douze pages** (dooz pahzh) — twelve pages
- **J'écris** (zhay-kree) — I write
- **j'ai peur** (zhay puhr) — I'm scared (literally: I have fear)
- **La règle a quarante ans** (lah reh-gluh ah kah-rahN-tahN) — The rule is forty years old (avoir for age; no z after quarante)
- **Pourquoi vous aimez Léa** (poor-kwah voo‿zeh-may lay-ah) — Why do you love Léa
- **Parce qu'elle rit** (pars kel ree) — Because she laughs (qu' before a vowel)
- **votre discours** (voh-truh dees-koor) — your speech (polite)
- **C'est tout** (seh too) — That's all

#### Notice: Pourquoi… ? Parce que…

Rose asks Pourquoi vous aimez Léa ? and Paul answers three times with parce que. Before a vowel, que becomes qu': Parce qu'elle rit, Parce qu'avec elle. Pourquoi asks for a reason; parce que gives it. See the table: Grammar tables, Question words.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Il ne faut pas chercher midi à quatorze heures. »** (eel nuh foh pah shair-shay mee-dee ah kah-tor-zuhr)

*Literally:* You mustn't look for noon at two p.m.

*Meaning:* Don't make a simple thing complicated.

*English equivalent:* Keep it simple.

### Episode 3 · Le petit-neveu (The great-nephew)

*On Saturday at five past eight, Hugo, Rose's 22-year-old great-nephew, runs into the café for his first day at work, in an apron that is too short, and drops a white cup. Socrate, the grey parrot by the window, fluffs up, offended. Hugo sweeps up the pieces, and Rose puts a new white cup on her side of the counter and looks at him over her glasses.*

**Hugo:** J'arrive ! Pardon, Tata !
> *Coming! Sorry, Auntie!* (worried)

**Rose:** Pas de problème. Une tasse, deux euros.
> *No problem. One cup: two euros.* (teasing)

**Hugo:** Un café, s'il te plaît. Je suis de la famille !
> *A coffee, please. I'm family!* (annoyed)

**Rose:** La règle, c'est la règle. Même pour toi.
> *Rules are rules. Even for you.* (teasing)

**Rose:** Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire, toi ?
> *And what do you like doing yourself?* (curious)

**Hugo:** J'aime faire des gâteaux. Mes parents aiment le droit.
> *I like baking cakes. My parents like law.* (sad)

**Hugo:** D'abord la tasse. Puis le café.
> *First the cup. Then the coffee.* (proud)

**Rose:** Voilà. Un café, puis un autre.
> *There you go. One coffee, then another.* (amused)

**Hugo:** Socrate a quel âge, Tata ?
> *How old is Socrate, Auntie?* (curious)

**Rose:** Cinquante ans ! Plus vieux que le Café des Questions.
> *Fifty! Older than the Café des Questions.* (neutral)

**Hugo:** Plus vieux que le café ? Le café a quel âge ?
> *Older than the café? How old is the café?* (surprised)

**Rose:** Ici, c'est moi qui pose les questions.
> *Here, I'm the one who asks the questions.* (teasing)

#### Words from this episode

- **J'arrive** (zhah-reev) — Coming! / I'm on my way
- **Pardon** (par-dohN) — Sorry
- **Pas de problème** (pah duh proh-blem) — No problem
- **s'il te plaît** (seel tuh pleh) — please (tu form; polite: s'il vous plaît)
- **Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire** (kes-kuh tew em fair) — What do you like doing (to family)
- **J'aime faire des gâteaux** (zhem fair day gah-toh) — I like baking cakes (aimer + infinitive)
- **le droit** (luh drwah) — law (the subject; le: masculine)
- **Socrate a quel âge** (soh-krat ah kel ahzh) — How old is Socrate (avoir for age)
- **Cinquante ans** (saN-kahN-tahN) — fifty years old (no z after cinquante)

#### Notice: Tu or vous: family and customers

Hugo and Rose are family, so they say tu: Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire, toi ?, s'il te plaît, Même pour toi. With customers Rose says vous, as in episodes 1 and 2: Qu'est-ce que vous aimez, le matin ? and Pourquoi vous aimez Léa ? So s'il te plaît becomes s'il vous plaît. See the table: Grammar tables, Subject pronouns.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid. »** (puh-tee‿tah puh-tee, lwah-zoh feh sohN nee)

*Literally:* Little by little, the bird makes its nest.

*Meaning:* Patience and small steps get big things done.

*English equivalent:* Slowly but surely.

### Episode 4 · Un jour à Paris (One day in Paris)

*On Tuesday at ten, Madame Rose is at the market, so Hugo is alone behind the counter. Emma, an English tourist, comes in with a printed plan: Paris in one day, minute by minute. Hugo puts her white cup on his side, like Rose, and when Emma looks at her plan he points at the window; she crosses out half of it. Socrate steals a sugar cube from her saucer, and behind the counter hangs a row of postcards of the sea.*

**Emma:** Bonjour ! Un café, vite. J'ai un plan.
> *Hello! A coffee, quickly. I have a plan.* (worried)

**Hugo:** Ici, une question, puis un café. Votre couleur préférée ?
> *Here, it's one question, then a coffee. Your favourite colour? (US: favorite color)* (teasing)

**Emma:** Le bleu ? C'est la règle ?
> *Blue? Is that the rule?* (amused)

**Hugo:** Non… pardon. Ma vraie question : qu'est-ce que vous voyez, là ?
> *No… sorry. My real question: what can you see, right there?* (curious)

**Emma:** Mon plan ! À dix heures douze, une photo du Sacré-Cœur.
> *My plan! At 10:12, a photo of the Sacré-Cœur.* (worried)

**Emma:** Oh… Je vois les toits. Et le Sacré-Cœur. C'est beau.
> *Oh… I can see the roofs. And the Sacré-Cœur. It's beautiful.* (moved)

**Emma:** Et ces cartes postales de la mer, là ? C'est où ?
> *And those postcards of the sea, over there? Where is that?* (curious)

**Hugo:** À Saint-Malo. Tata Rose reçoit une carte chaque année.
> *In Saint-Malo. Auntie Rose gets a card every year.* (neutral)

**Emma:** De qui ?
> *Who from?* (curious)

**Hugo:** Je ne sais pas. Mystère !
> *I don't know. It's a mystery!* (amused)

**Emma:** Je reste. Un autre café, s'il vous plaît.
> *I'm staying. Another coffee, please.* (relieved)

#### Words from this episode

- **J'ai un plan** (zhay uhN plahN) — I have a plan
- **Votre couleur préférée** (voh-truh koo-luhr pray-fay-ray) — your favourite colour (US: favorite color)
- **qu'est-ce que vous voyez** (kes-kuh voo vwah-yay) — what can you see (voir)
- **À dix heures douze** (ah dee‿zuhr dooz) — at 10:12 (à + the time)
- **du Sacré-Cœur** (dew sah-kray-kuhr) — of the Sacré-Cœur (de + le = du)
- **reçoit une carte** (ruh-swah ewn kart) — gets a card (recevoir)
- **chaque année** (shahk ah-nay) — every year
- **Je ne sais pas** (zhuh nuh seh pah) — I don't know
- **Je reste** (zhuh rest) — I'm staying
- **s'il vous plaît** (seel voo pleh) — please (polite)

#### Notice: Telling the time: à dix heures douze

Emma's plan uses à + the time: À dix heures douze, une photo du Sacré-Cœur. Say the hour, then heures, then the minutes: dix heures douze is 10:12. Noon is midi, with no heures. See the table: Grammar tables, Telling the time.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Paris ne s'est pas fait en un jour. »** (pah-ree nuh seh pah feh ahN‿nuhN zhoor)

*Literally:* Paris wasn't made in one day.

*Meaning:* Great things take time and patience; you can't do them all at once.

*English equivalent:* Rome wasn't built in a day.

### Episode 5 · Monsieur Oui (Mister Yes)

*On Friday morning Antoine comes into Madame Rose's café with his neighbour's dog on a lead, his boss's files and his sister's shopping. He says yes before anyone speaks, and he even says sorry to Socrate, the grey parrot by the window. Rose puts the white cup on her side of the counter and taps the slate.*

**Antoine:** Bonjour ! Oui, oui, d'accord !
> *Hello! Yes, yes, OK!* (worried)

**Rose:** Mais je ne demande rien, monsieur !
> *But I'm not asking anything!* (teasing)

**Antoine:** Ah… oui. Pardon. Pardon aussi, monsieur le perroquet !
> *Ah… right. Sorry. Sorry to you too, Mr Parrot!* (worried)

**Rose:** Vous dites pardon à Socrate ?
> *You're saying sorry to Socrate?* (amused)

**Antoine:** Je dis toujours oui. Mon chef, ma sœur, votre règle…
> *I always say yes. My boss, my sister, your rule…* (sad)

**Rose:** Ce n'est pas ma règle. Elle est à une amie.
> *It isn't my rule. It belongs to a friend.* (neutral)

**Rose:** Et vous, qu'est-ce que vous voulez ?
> *And you, what do you want?* (curious)

**Antoine:** Moi ? Je… Je ne veux pas garder le chien !
> *Me? I… I don't want to look after the dog!* (surprised)

**Antoine:** Et je n'aime pas les chiens.
> *And I don't like dogs.* (relieved)

**Rose:** Vous ne dites jamais non. Alors, c'est toujours oui.
> *You never say no. So it's always yes.* (amused)

**Rose:** Une part de tarte ? Cinq euros.
> *A slice of tart? Five euros.* (teasing)

**Antoine:** Non ! Non, merci. Mon premier non !
> *No! No, thank you. My first no!* (proud)

#### Words from this episode

- **D'accord** (dah-kor) — OK, all right
- **Je ne demande rien** (zhuh nuh duh-mahNd ryaN) — I'm not asking anything (ne… rien: nothing)
- **Pardon** (par-dohN) — Sorry
- **Je dis toujours oui** (zhuh dee too-zhoor wee) — I always say yes (dire: je dis)
- **ma règle** (mah reh-gluh) — my rule (ma: feminine)
- **Et vous** (ay voo) — And you? (vous after et: stressed form)
- **qu'est-ce que vous voulez** (kes-kuh voo voo-lay) — what do you want
- **Je ne veux pas** (zhuh nuh vuh pah) — I don't want (ne + verb + pas)
- **Je n'aime pas les chiens** (zhuh nem pah lay shyaN) — I don't like dogs (n' before a vowel)
- **Cinq euros** (saN-kuh-roh) — five euros (no z after cinq)

#### Notice: Saying no: ne… pas

Antoine finally says Je ne veux pas garder le chien ! and Je n'aime pas les chiens. Ne goes before the verb and pas after it; before a vowel, ne becomes n'. Rose's Vous ne dites jamais non works the same way, with jamais (never) instead of pas. See the table: Grammar tables, Negative words.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Qui ne dit mot consent. »** (kee nuh dee moh kohN-sahN)

*Literally:* Who says no word consents.

*Meaning:* If you say nothing, people think you agree.

*English equivalent:* Silence gives consent.

## Act 2 · Ce qui s'est passé (What happened)

*Level A2*

### Episode 6 · Le permis (The driving test)

*On a Thursday morning Léo, seventeen, drops into a chair in Rose's tiny Montmartre café: he has just failed his driving test. Rose puts a white cup on her side of the counter and points at the slate by the door. When Léo tells the truth, Socrate the grey parrot fluffs up his feathers.*

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. Vous voulez un chocolat chaud ?
> *Hello, sir. Would you like a hot chocolate?* (neutral)

**Léo:** Vous ? Moi ? Personne ne me dit vous !
> *'Vous'? To me? Nobody says 'vous' to me!* (surprised)

**Rose:** Ici, je dis vous à tout le monde. Même à Socrate.
> *Here I say 'vous' to everyone. Even to Socrate.* (teasing)

**Léo:** J'ai raté mon permis ce matin. Je suis nul.
> *I failed my driving test this morning. I'm useless. (US: driver's test)* (sad)

**Rose:** Nul ? Vous avez dix-sept ans, monsieur.
> *Useless? You're seventeen, sir.* (amused)

**Léo:** Je suis parti trop vite. L'examinateur a crié. J'en ai marre !
> *I pulled away too fast. The examiner shouted. I'm fed up!* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Alors, ma question. Qu'est-ce que vous avez appris ce matin ?
> *So, my question. What did you learn this morning?* (curious)

**Léo:** J'ai appris… à regarder à droite. Et à partir doucement.
> *I learnt… to look to the right. And to pull away gently. (US: learned)* (relieved)

**Rose:** Moi aussi, j'ai raté un examen. Ce n'est pas grave.
> *I failed an exam once too. It doesn't matter.* (neutral)

**Léo:** Je vais repasser le permis en juin. Et vous, alors ?
> *I'm going to retake the test in June. And what about you, then?* (hopeful)

**Rose:** Alors ? Je suis là. Et je suis contente.
> *Then? I'm here. And I'm happy.* (proud)

#### Words from this episode

- **J'ai raté mon permis** (zhay rah-tay mohN pair-mee) — I failed my driving test (rater: avoir in the passé composé)
- **dix-sept ans** (dee-se-tahN) — seventeen (years old) (avoir dix-sept ans; no z after sept)
- **Je suis parti** (zhuh swee par-tee) — I left / I pulled away (partir takes être)
- **J'en ai marre !** (zhahN‿nay mar) — I'm fed up! (informal)
- **Qu'est-ce que vous avez appris** (kes-kuh voo‿zah-vay ah-pree) — What did you learn (apprendre → appris)
- **regarder à droite** (ruh-gar-day ah drwaht) — to look to the right
- **partir doucement** (par-teer doos-mahN) — to pull away gently
- **Ce n'est pas grave** (suh neh pah grahv) — It doesn't matter (spoken: c'est pas grave)
- **Je vais repasser le permis** (zhuh veh ruh-pah-say luh pair-mee) — I'm going to retake the test (aller + infinitive)

#### Notice: Être or avoir: je suis parti, j'ai raté

Léo says J'ai raté mon permis and J'ai appris à regarder, but Je suis parti trop vite. Most verbs make the passé composé with avoir; partir is one of the être verbs (aller, arriver, partir, rester, tomber…). With être the participle agrees: Rose would say je suis partie. See the table: Grammar tables, Verbs that take être in the passé composé.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron. »** (seh‿tahN for-zhahN kohN duh-vyaN for-zhuh-rohN)

*Literally:* It's by forging that you become a blacksmith.

*Meaning:* You learn by doing it again and again, mistakes included.

*English equivalent:* Practice makes perfect.

---

### Episode 7 · L'influenceur (The influencer)

*On a Saturday afternoon Max, an influencer, walks into Rose's tiny Montmartre café filming himself. Rose waits behind the counter while Hugo works in the small kitchen. When Max holds up his phone for a selfie with Socrate, the grey parrot turns his back. Rose keeps the white cup on her side until Max answers.*

**Max:** Salut tout le monde ! Je suis au café secret. C'est génial !
> *Hi everyone! I'm at the secret café. It's brilliant!* (proud)

**Rose:** Ici, on dit bonjour à la dame.
> *Here, we say hello to the lady.* (teasing)

**Max:** Pardon ! Bonjour, madame. J'ai deux cent mille abonnés !
> *Sorry! Hello, madam. I've got two hundred thousand followers!* (amused)

**Rose:** Moi, j'ai un perroquet. Il ne m'aime pas non plus.
> *I've got a parrot. He doesn't like me either.* (teasing)

**Max:** Un selfie avec lui ? Oh ! Il m'a tourné le dos !
> *A selfie with him? Oh! He's turned his back on me!* (surprised)

**Rose:** Socrate a connu la première patronne. Il n'aime pas les photos.
> *Socrate knew the first owner. He doesn't like photos.* (amused)

**Max:** Bon, bon. Et la question, je la filme ?
> *All right, all right. And the question, shall I film it?* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Non, vous la vivez. Qu'avez-vous vu aujourd'hui ? Pas filmé : vu.
> *No, you live it. What have you seen today? Not filmed: seen.* (curious)

**Max:** J'ai vu… mon téléphone. Je n'ai pas regardé Paris.
> *I saw… my phone. I didn't look at Paris.* (sad)

**Rose:** Votre café, monsieur. Paris est là, derrière la fenêtre.
> *Your coffee, sir. Paris is right there, behind the window.* (neutral)

**Max:** Je vais rester un peu. Sans vidéo.
> *I'm going to stay a while. No video.* (relieved)

#### Words from this episode

- **C'est génial !** (seh zhay-nyahl) — It's brilliant! (US: awesome)
- **on dit bonjour** (ohN dee bohN-zhoor) — we say hello (on = people in general)
- **deux cent mille abonnés** (duh sahN meel ah-bu-nay) — two hundred thousand followers (cent, mille: no -s here)
- **Il ne m'aime pas non plus** (eel nuh mem pah nohN plew) — He doesn't like me either
- **Il m'a tourné le dos** (eel mah toor-nay luh doh) — He's turned his back on me
- **Socrate a connu** (soh-krat ah koh-new) — Socrate knew (connaître → connu)
- **Qu'avez-vous vu** (kah-vay voo vew) — What have you seen? (voir → vu)
- **Je n'ai pas regardé Paris** (zhuh nay pah ruh-gar-day pah-ree) — I didn't look at Paris (ne… pas around ai)
- **Je vais rester un peu** (zhuh veh res-tay uhN puh) — I'm going to stay a while (aller + infinitive)

#### Notice: Ne… pas in the past: je n'ai pas regardé

Max says Je n'ai pas regardé Paris. In the passé composé, ne… pas goes around the auxiliary (n'ai pas), and the past participle comes after it. Rien works the same way (je n'ai rien vu), while in the present ne… pas goes around the verb itself: Il n'aime pas les photos. See the table: Grammar tables, Where the negative goes.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or. »** (too suh kee breey neh pah or)

*Literally:* All that shines is not gold.

*Meaning:* Things that look wonderful aren't always what they seem.

*English equivalent:* All that glitters is not gold.

---

### Episode 8 · Le vélo (The bicycle)

*On a Monday morning Bruno, in a grey suit, stares into his white cup at the counter of Rose's Montmartre café before it is even full. There is a little black bike grease on his hands. Rose keeps the cup on her side until he answers, and Socrate the parrot steals Bruno's sugar cube.*

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. Vous avez l'air triste.
> *Hello, sir. You look sad.* (neutral)

**Bruno:** C'est lundi.
> *It's Monday.* (sad)

**Rose:** C'est lundi ? Ah. Ça explique tout.
> *It's Monday? Ah. That explains everything.* (teasing)

**Bruno:** Je travaille dans les assurances depuis vingt-cinq ans. J'en ai assez.
> *I've worked in insurance for twenty-five years. I've had enough.* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Quand est-ce que vous avez été heureux, la semaine dernière ?
> *When were you happy, last week?* (curious)

**Bruno:** Samedi, j'ai réparé le vélo de mon voisin. Quatre heures !
> *On Saturday I repaired my neighbour's bike. Four hours! (US: neighbor's)* (surprised)

**Bruno:** C'est bête, quand même. Un vélo… Mais j'ai été heureux.
> *It's silly, though. A bike… But I was happy.* (moved)

**Rose:** Pas bête. Moi aussi, j'ai changé de vie. Il y a longtemps.
> *Not silly. I changed my life too. A long time ago.* (neutral)

**Bruno:** Ah bon ? Pourquoi ?
> *Really? Why?* (curious)

**Rose:** Ici, c'est moi qui pose les questions.
> *Here, I'm the one who asks the questions.* (teasing)

**Bruno:** Du coup, je vais passer au magasin de vélos, rue Lepic.
> *So I'm going to drop by the bike shop on rue Lepic.* (hopeful)

#### Words from this episode

- **Je travaille** (zhuh trah-vahy) — I work (travailler)
- **depuis vingt-cinq ans** (duh-pwee vaNt-saN-kahN) — for twenty-five years (and still now: depuis + present)
- **vous avez été** (voo‿zah-vay ay-tay) — you were / you have been (être → été)
- **la semaine dernière** (lah suh-men dair-nyair) — last week (like l'année dernière)
- **quand même** (kahN mem) — though / all the same
- **j'ai changé de vie** (zhay shahN-zhay duh vee) — I changed my life (changer de + noun, no article)
- **Du coup** (dew koo) — So / as a result (spoken)
- **je vais passer** (zhuh veh pah-say) — I'm going to drop by (aller + infinitive)

#### Notice: Time words: depuis, il y a, la semaine dernière

Bruno says Je travaille dans les assurances depuis vingt-cinq ans: depuis + the present means it started then and is still going on. Rose says J'ai changé de vie. Il y a longtemps: il y a + a time means ago, with the passé composé. La semaine dernière (last week) is built like the table's l'année dernière. See the table: Grammar tables, Common time expressions.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Il n'y a pas de sot métier. »** (eel nyah pah duh soh may-tyay)

*Literally:* There's no stupid job.

*Meaning:* Every honest job deserves respect; none is beneath anyone.

*English equivalent:* There's no shame in honest work.

---

### Episode 9 · L'appel (The phone call)

*On a Tuesday morning Rose is at the market, so Hugo runs the counter of the Montmartre café, wearing his great-aunt's reading glasses to look serious; they keep slipping down his nose. Inès, a nurse still in her tunic after a night shift, puts her phone on the table, picks it up and puts it down again. When she says ma mère, Socrate the parrot fluffs up his feathers, and Hugo glances at the slate signed O. Later Inès steps outside with her phone and comes back with red eyes and a smile.*

**Hugo:** Bonjour, madame. Ici, une question, puis un café.
> *Hello, madam. Here: one question, then a coffee.* (proud)

**Inès:** Je suis fatiguée. J'ai travaillé toute la nuit.
> *I'm tired. I worked all night.* (sad)

**Hugo:** Oups. Les lunettes de Tata Rose. C'est pour avoir l'air sérieux.
> *Oops. Auntie Rose's glasses. They're to make me look serious.* (surprised)

**Inès:** Vous êtes drôle. D'accord, je vous écoute.
> *You're funny. All right, I'm listening.* (amused)

**Hugo:** Vous attendez un appel de qui ?
> *Whose call are you waiting for?* (curious)

**Inès:** De ma mère. On s'est disputées il y a trois mois.
> *My mother's. We had a row three months ago. (US: a fight)* (sad)

**Hugo:** Et vous, vous l'avez appelée ? Dimanche, c'est la fête des Mères.
> *And you, have you called her? Sunday is Mother's Day.* (hopeful)

**Inès:** Non. Elle ne m'a pas appelée non plus. J'attends.
> *No. She hasn't called me either. I'm waiting.* (annoyed)

**Hugo:** La règle vient d'une dame, Odette. Tata Rose ne parle jamais d'elle.
> *The rule comes from a lady, Odette. Auntie Rose never talks about her.* (neutral)

**Inès:** Je vais l'appeler tout de suite. Et je vais lui dire pardon.
> *I'm going to call her right now. And I'm going to say sorry to her.* (hopeful)

**Inès:** Elle a pleuré. Moi aussi. Et maintenant, mon café, s'il vous plaît !
> *She cried. So did I. And now, my coffee, please!* (relieved)

#### Words from this episode

- **Je suis fatiguée** (zhuh swee fah-tee-gay) — I'm tired (fatiguée: a woman speaking)
- **J'ai travaillé toute la nuit** (zhay trah-vah-yay toot lah nwee) — I worked all night
- **Vous attendez un appel** (voo‿zah-tahN-day uhN‿nah-pel) — You're waiting for a call (attendre: no word for 'for')
- **il y a trois mois** (eel ee ah trwah mwah) — three months ago (il y a = ago)
- **vous l'avez appelée** (voo lah-vay ah-puh-lay) — have you called her? (l' = her, so appelée agrees)
- **Je vais l'appeler** (zhuh veh lah-puh-lay) — I'm going to call her (l' before the infinitive)
- **tout de suite** (too duh sweet) — right now / straight away
- **je vais lui dire pardon** (zhuh veh lwee deer par-dohN) — I'm going to say sorry to her (lui = to her)
- **Elle a pleuré** (el ah pluh-ray) — She cried (pleurer)

#### Notice: L' or lui? Je vais l'appeler, je vais lui dire

Inès says Je vais l'appeler and Je vais lui dire pardon. Appeler takes a direct object (appeler sa mère → l'appeler), but dire takes à (dire pardon à sa mère → lui dire pardon). In the passé composé, a direct object before avoir makes the participle agree: vous l'avez appelée, elle ne m'a pas appelée. See the table: Grammar tables, Indirect object pronouns: me, lui, leur...

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Mieux vaut tard que jamais. »** (myuh voh tar kuh zhah-meh)

*Literally:* Late is worth more than never.

*Meaning:* It's better to do something late than not at all.

*English equivalent:* Better late than never.

---

### Episode 10 · La vieille photo (The old photo)

*On a Wednesday Victor, an amateur historian with a notebook, walks into Rose's Montmartre café already asking questions. Rose puts the white cup on her side of the counter and counts his questions on her fingers, and after the fifth one Socrate the parrot turns his back. In his bag Victor has a photo from 1975 that he bought at a flea market on Sunday: a woman in a big hat in front of this door. Above the door, the old name is still faint under the new sign.*

**Victor:** Bonjour ! Le café a quel âge ? Le comptoir est d'origine ?
> *Hello! How old is the café? Is the counter original?* (curious)

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. Ça fait deux questions.
> *Hello, sir. That's two questions.* (teasing)

**Victor:** Et le perroquet ? Il parle ? Vous êtes là depuis quand ?
> *And the parrot? Does he talk? How long have you been here?* (curious)

**Rose:** Cinq. Regardez, Socrate vous tourne le dos.
> *Five. Look, Socrate is turning his back on you.* (amused)

**Victor:** Pardon ! J'écris un blog sur le vieux Montmartre.
> *Sorry! I write a blog about old Montmartre.* (proud)

**Rose:** Une question. Une. C'est moi qui la pose.
> *One question. One. And I'm the one who asks it.* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Qu'est-ce que votre femme vous a dit ce matin ?
> *What did your wife say to you this morning?* (curious)

**Victor:** Ma femme ? Je ne sais pas. Je n'ai pas écouté.
> *My wife? I don't know. I didn't listen.* (surprised)

**Rose:** Votre café, monsieur. Vous l'avez mérité.
> *Your coffee, sir. You've earned it.* (teasing)

**Victor:** Merci. Regardez ! Sur la photo, le café s'appelle Chez Odette.
> *Thank you. Look! In the photo, the café is called Chez Odette.* (curious)

**Rose:** Odette… Vous avez trouvé Odette.
> *Odette… You've found Odette.* (moved)

**Victor:** Ce soir, je vais écouter ma femme. Une heure. Sans carnet.
> *Tonight I'm going to listen to my wife. For an hour. No notebook.* (hopeful)

#### Words from this episode

- **Le café a quel âge** (luh kah-fay ah kel ahzh) — How old is the café? (avoir + age)
- **Pardon** (par-dohN) — Sorry / excuse me
- **J'écris un blog** (zhay-kree uhN blog) — I write a blog (écrire)
- **votre femme vous a dit** (voh-truh fahm voo‿zah dee) — your wife said to you (dire → dit)
- **Je n'ai pas écouté** (zhuh nay pah ay-koo-tay) — I didn't listen (écouter)
- **Vous l'avez mérité** (voo lah-vay may-ree-tay) — You've earned it (l' = the coffee)
- **Vous avez trouvé Odette** (voo‿zah-vay troo-vay oh-det) — You've found Odette (trouver)
- **Ce soir** (suh swahr) — This evening / tonight (ce = this)
- **je vais écouter** (zhuh veh ay-koo-tay) — I'm going to listen (aller + infinitive)

#### Notice: The near future: je vais écouter

Victor ends with Ce soir, je vais écouter ma femme: the present of aller (je vais, vous allez, elle va) + an infinitive says what is going to happen. In speech it is much more common than the futur simple in the table (j'écouterai). Inès did the same last time: Je vais l'appeler. See the table: Grammar tables, Futur simple: endings and irregular stems.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Il n'est pire sourd que celui qui ne veut pas entendre. »** (eel neh peer soor kuh suh-lwee kee nuh vuh pah ahN-tahN-druh)

*Literally:* There's no worse deaf man than the one who doesn't want to hear.

*Meaning:* The hardest person to reach is the one who won't listen.

*English equivalent:* There are none so deaf as those who will not hear.

---

## Act 3 · Les souvenirs (Memories (A2+))

*Level A2*

### Episode 11 · Le bal du samedi (Saturday dances)

*On a Monday morning in June, an old man with a cane stops at the door of the tiny Montmartre café and stares at the slate. Albert, 82, used to deliver the post on this street, and he recognises Madame Rose before she recognises him. He orders a white coffee; Rose puts the white cup on her side of the counter and taps the slate. On his perch, Socrate fluffs up his feathers for Albert.*

**Albert:** Mademoiselle Rose ? La petite étudiante ? Moi, c'est Albert, le facteur !
> *Miss Rose? The little student? It's me, Albert, the postman! (US: mailman)* (surprised)

**Rose:** Albert ! Le facteur ! Ça fait presque cinquante ans !
> *Albert! The postman! It's been almost fifty years!* (moved)

**Albert:** Vous étiez toujours pressée. Vous buviez votre café debout.
> *You were always in a hurry. You drank your coffee standing up.* (amused)

**Albert:** Un matin, Odette vous a posé une question. C'était quoi ?
> *One morning, Odette asked you a question. What was it?* (curious)

**Rose:** Ici, c'est moi qui pose les questions.
> *Here, I'm the one who asks the questions.* (teasing)

**Rose:** Qu'est-ce que vous aimiez faire le samedi soir ?
> *What did you like to do on Saturday nights?* (curious)

**Albert:** Je dansais ! Au bal, place des Abbesses. Je dansais très bien.
> *I used to dance! At the dance, on the place des Abbesses. I danced very well.* (proud)

**Albert:** Mais maintenant, j'ai quatre-vingt-deux ans. Je suis trop vieux.
> *But now I'm eighty-two. I'm too old.* (sad)

**Rose:** Vous devriez danser encore. Il y a un bal samedi, à la mairie.
> *You should dance again. There's a dance on Saturday, at the town hall.* (hopeful)

**Albert:** D'accord ! Mais vous venez avec moi, mademoiselle Rose ?
> *All right! But will you come with me, Miss Rose?* (hopeful)

**Rose:** Moi ? Oh non, je suis trop vieille !
> *Me? Oh no, I'm too old!* (surprised)

**Albert:** Ah non ! Pas vous aussi !
> *Oh no! Not you too!* (amused)

#### Words from this episode

- **Vous étiez toujours pressée** (voo‿zay-tyay too-zhoor preh-say) — You were always in a hurry (étiez: imparfait of être)
- **Vous buviez votre café debout** (voo bew-vyay voh-truh kah-fay duh-boo) — You used to drink your coffee standing up (boire: nous buvons → vous buviez)
- **Ça fait presque cinquante ans** (sah feh presk saN-kahN-tahN) — It's been almost fifty years (cinquante ans: no z)
- **c'est moi qui pose les questions** (seh mwah kee pohz lay kes-tyohN) — I'm the one who asks the questions
- **Qu'est-ce que vous aimiez faire** (kes-kuh voo‿zeh-myay fair) — What did you like to do (aimiez: imparfait)
- **j'ai quatre-vingt-deux ans** (zhay kah-truh-vaN-duh‿zahN) — I'm eighty-two (avoir for age)
- **Vous devriez danser** (voo duh-vree-yay dahN-say) — You should dance (vous devriez + infinitive: advice)
- **D'accord** (dah-kor) — All right / OK
- **je suis trop vieille** (zhuh swee troh vyey) — I'm too old (vieux → vieille for a woman)

#### Notice: The imparfait: vous étiez, je dansais

Albert remembers: Vous étiez toujours pressée. Vous buviez votre café debout. Je dansais très bien. Habits and descriptions in the past take the imparfait: the nous stem (nous buvons → buv-) plus -ais, -ait, -iez, with être as the one irregular stem (ét-). For one single event Albert uses the passé composé: Un matin, Odette vous a posé une question. See the table: Grammar tables, Imparfait: how things were, what used to happen.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« C'est dans les vieux pots qu'on fait les meilleures soupes. »** (seh dahN lay vyuh poh kohN feh lay meh-yuhr soop)

*Literally:* It's in the old pots that you make the best soups.

*Meaning:* Experience and age are an advantage, not a weakness.

*English equivalent:* There's many a good tune played on an old fiddle.

---

### Episode 12 · Le gâteau brûlé (The burnt cake)

*On Tuesday morning, while Rose is at the market, Hugo runs the tiny Montmartre café alone. Nadia, a pharmacist, puts a black, burnt three-tier cake on the counter. On his perch, Socrate turns his back on the cake, and Hugo puts the white cup on his side of the counter, just like his great-aunt. At the end, Nadia ties on an apron and Socrate helps himself to the apples.*

**Nadia:** Bonjour. Voilà mon gâteau. Enfin… c'était mon gâteau.
> *Hello. Here's my cake. Well… it was my cake.* (annoyed)

**Hugo:** Oh là là ! Même Socrate ne veut pas le regarder !
> *Oh dear! Even Socrate won't look at it!* (amused)

**Nadia:** C'est pour ma fille, Lina. Elle va avoir huit ans samedi.
> *It's for my daughter, Lina. She's going to be eight on Saturday.* (sad)

**Nadia:** Le gâteau du magazine… Trois étages, des décorations en or. Brûlé deux fois !
> *The cake from the magazine… Three tiers, gold decorations. Burnt twice!* (annoyed)

**Hugo:** Bon. Ici, une question, puis un café. Même pour un gâteau brûlé.
> *Right. Here: one question, then a coffee. Even for a burnt cake.* (teasing)

**Hugo:** Quand Lina était petite, qu'est-ce qu'elle aimait manger ?
> *When Lina was little, what did she like to eat?* (curious)

**Nadia:** Elle adorait la tarte aux pommes de sa grand-mère.
> *She loved her grandmother's apple tart.* (moved)

**Nadia:** Simple. Avec du beurre et du sucre.
> *Simple. With butter and sugar.* (surprised)

**Hugo:** Il faut faire simple. Vous devriez faire une tarte aux pommes.
> *You have to keep it simple. You should make an apple tart.* (hopeful)

**Nadia:** Une tarte ? Mais je ne sais pas faire les tartes !
> *A tart? But I don't know how to make tarts!* (worried)

**Hugo:** Tata Rose fait la tarte d'Odette depuis quarante ans. Elle m'a appris la recette.
> *Auntie Rose has been making Odette's tart for forty years. She taught me the recipe.* (proud)

**Hugo:** Ce n'est pas la mer à boire. Je vous montre ?
> *It's not that hard. Shall I show you? (literally: it's not the sea to drink)* (hopeful)

**Nadia:** D'accord ! Mais regardez Socrate : il mange déjà les pommes !
> *All right! But look at Socrate: he's already eating the apples!* (amused)

#### Words from this episode

- **c'était mon gâteau** (say-teh mohN gah-toh) — it was my cake (c'était: imparfait of c'est)
- **Enfin** (ahN-faN) — Well… / I mean (correcting yourself)
- **huit ans** (wee‿tahN) — eight years old (huit + ans: t liaison)
- **qu'est-ce qu'elle aimait manger** (kes-kel eh-meh mahN-zhay) — what did she like to eat (aimait: imparfait)
- **du beurre et du sucre** (dew buhr ay dew sew-kruh) — butter and sugar (du: some, partitive)
- **Il faut faire simple** (eel foh fair saN-pluh) — You have to keep it simple (il faut + infinitive)
- **Vous devriez faire une tarte aux pommes** (voo duh-vree-yay fair ewn tart oh pum) — You should make an apple tart (advice)
- **Elle m'a appris la recette** (el mah ah-pree lah ruh-set) — She taught me the recipe (apprendre quelque chose à quelqu'un)
- **Ce n'est pas la mer à boire** (suh neh pah lah mair ah bwahr) — It's not that hard
- **Je vous montre ?** (zhuh voo mohN-truh) — Shall I show you?

#### Notice: Giving advice: il faut, vous devriez

Hugo gives advice two ways: Il faut faire simple and Vous devriez faire une tarte aux pommes. Il faut + infinitive states a general rule (you have to), while vous devriez + infinitive, devoir in the conditional, is a softer, personal suggestion (you should). To a friend it's tu devrais: Tu devrais essayer. See the table: Grammar tables, Conditional: would, could, polite requests.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Le mieux est l'ennemi du bien. »** (luh myuh eh len-mee dew byaN)

*Literally:* The best is the enemy of the good.

*Meaning:* Trying to make something perfect can spoil what was already good.

*English equivalent:* Perfect is the enemy of good.

---

### Episode 13 · Pourquoi, pourquoi, pourquoi (Why, why, why)

*On Friday at eight, Samuel collapses at one of the three little tables of the Montmartre café. Every morning he walks past the window with his son Noé, six, who asks 'why' from seven o'clock. Rose puts the white cup on her side of the counter and looks at him over her glasses. Socrate, silent as always, watches from his perch by the window.*

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. Vous avez l'air fatigué.
> *Good morning. You look tired.* (teasing)

**Samuel:** Un café. Double. Ne me posez pas de question.
> *A coffee. A double. Don't ask me any questions.* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Ah, ça, c'est impossible. Ici, une question, puis un café.
> *Ah, that's impossible. Here: one question, then a coffee.* (amused)

**Samuel:** Mon fils a six ans. Ce matin : « Pourquoi le perroquet ne dit rien ? »
> *My son is six. This morning: 'Why doesn't the parrot say anything?'* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Il réfléchit. Socrate réfléchit depuis cinquante ans.
> *He's thinking. Socrate has been thinking for fifty years.* (amused)

**Rose:** Et vous, quand vous étiez petit, vous posiez des questions ?
> *And you, when you were little, did you ask questions?* (curious)

**Samuel:** Oui… tout le temps. Et mon père disait : « Parce que. »
> *Yes… all the time. And my father used to say: 'Because.'* (sad)

**Samuel:** Je n'aimais pas ça… Et moi, je dis la même chose !
> *I didn't like that… And I say the same thing!* (surprised)

**Rose:** Quand j'étais jeune, je ne posais pas de questions. Je courais.
> *When I was young, I didn't ask questions. I ran.* (moved)

**Samuel:** Alors, qu'est-ce que je dois faire ?
> *So what should I do?* (curious)

**Rose:** Vous devriez lui poser une question, à lui.
> *You should be the one asking him a question.* (neutral)

**Rose:** « Et toi, pourquoi tu penses que le ciel est bleu ? »
> *'And you, why do you think the sky is blue?'* (teasing)

**Samuel:** Alors, moi, je vais lui demander : « Et toi ? »
> *So I'm going to ask him: 'And you?'* (hopeful)

#### Words from this episode

- **fatigué** (fah-tee-gay) — tired (Vous avez l'air fatigué: you look tired)
- **Ne me posez pas de question** (nuh muh poh-zay pah duh kes-tyohN) — Don't ask me any questions
- **vous posiez des questions** (voo poh-zyay day kes-tyohN) — you used to ask questions (posiez: imparfait)
- **mon père disait** (mohN pair dee-zeh) — my father used to say (dire: imparfait)
- **Et moi** (ay mwah) — And me / And I (moi: stressed pronoun)
- **qu'est-ce que je dois faire** (kes-kuh zhuh dwah fair) — what should I do (devoir: must, should)
- **Vous devriez lui poser une question** (voo duh-vree-yay lwee poh-zay ewn kes-tyohN) — You should ask him a question (advice)
- **tu penses que** (tew pahNs kuh) — you think that (tu: to a child)

#### Notice: Stressed pronouns: moi, toi, lui, vous

Rose asks Et vous, quand vous étiez petit… ? and Samuel answers Et moi, je dis la même chose ! After et, on their own, or to stress a person, French uses moi, toi, lui, vous instead of je, tu, il: Alors, moi…, une question, à lui. Et toi ? is tu because it's what Samuel will say to his six-year-old son; Rose and Samuel still say vous to each other. See the table: Grammar tables, Stressed pronouns: moi, toi...

#### Sagesse du jour

**« La vérité sort de la bouche des enfants. »** (lah vay-ree-tay sor duh lah boosh day‿zahN-fahN)

*Literally:* The truth comes out of children's mouths.

*Meaning:* Children often say simple true things that adults avoid.

*English equivalent:* Out of the mouths of babes.

---

### Episode 14 · La carte postale (The postcard)

*On Tuesday 23 June, Madame Rose's seventieth birthday, Rose is at the market and Hugo runs the Montmartre café alone. Juliette, the street's postwoman, comes in with the post, a camera hanging from her bag. Hugo's thick law textbook (Droit civil) lies open on the counter next to the till; later, Juliette sees it and turns Hugo's question back on him. Socrate tries to eat the postcard, so Hugo hides it in the sugar bowl, then puts the white cup on his side of the counter.*

**Juliette:** Bonjour ! Une carte pour Madame Rose. De Saint-Malo, comme chaque année.
> *Hello! A card for Madame Rose. From Saint-Malo, like every year.* (neutral)

**Hugo:** « Bon anniversaire, Rose. Tu cours encore ? O. »
> *'Happy birthday, Rose. Are you still running? O.'* (curious)

**Hugo:** O… Odette ! Elle est à Saint-Malo ! Elle écrit chaque année !
> *O… Odette! She's in Saint-Malo! She writes every year!* (surprised)

**Juliette:** Attention ! Socrate veut manger la carte !
> *Watch out! Socrate wants to eat the card!* (amused)

**Hugo:** Bon. Un café pour la factrice ? Ici, une question, puis un café.
> *Right. A coffee for the postwoman? Here: one question, then a coffee.* (teasing)

**Hugo:** Qu'est-ce que vous vouliez faire, quand vous étiez petite ?
> *What did you want to do when you were little?* (curious)

**Juliette:** Je voulais être photographe. Je prenais des photos de tout.
> *I wanted to be a photographer. I took photos of everything.* (moved)

**Hugo:** Mais vous avez un appareil photo ! Vous devriez essayer.
> *But you've got a camera! You should try.* (hopeful)

**Juliette:** Et vous, vous aimez le droit ?
> *And you, do you like law?* (teasing)

**Hugo:** Moi ? Euh… Mes parents aiment le droit.
> *Me? Er… My parents like law.* (surprised)

**Hugo:** Moi, j'aime faire des gâteaux…
> *What I like is making cakes…* (sad)

**Juliette:** C'est génial ! Vous devriez essayer, vous aussi.
> *That's great! You should try too.* (hopeful)

**Juliette:** Souriez ! Une photo avec la carte. Pour Madame Rose, pour ses soixante-dix ans.
> *Smile! A photo with the card. For Madame Rose, for her seventieth birthday.* (proud)

#### Words from this episode

- **comme chaque année** (kohm shahk ah-nay) — like every year
- **Tu cours encore ?** (tew koor ahN-kor) — Are you still running? (tu: old friends)
- **Elle écrit chaque année** (el ay-kree shahk ah-nay) — She writes every year
- **Qu'est-ce que vous vouliez faire** (kes-kuh voo voo-lyay fair) — What did you want to do (vouliez: imparfait of vouloir)
- **Je voulais être photographe** (zhuh voo-leh eh-truh foh-toh-grahf) — I wanted to be a photographer (a past dream: imparfait)
- **Je prenais des photos** (zhuh pruh-neh day foh-toh) — I used to take photos (prendre: imparfait)
- **Vous devriez essayer** (voo duh-vree-yay eh-seh-yay) — You should try (advice)
- **vous aimez le droit** (voo‿zeh-may luh drwah) — you like law (le droit: law, the subject)
- **C'est génial !** (seh zhay-nyahl) — That's great!
- **ses soixante-dix ans** (say swah-sahNt-dee‿zahN) — her seventieth birthday (ses: her, before a plural noun)

#### Notice: Imparfait or passé composé: je voulais, elle a écrit

Juliette describes her childhood dream: Je voulais être photographe. Je prenais des photos de tout. A dream or a habit in the past takes the imparfait, but one finished event takes the passé composé: Odette a écrit une carte. The postcard says Tu cours encore ? in tu because Odette and Rose are old friends; Hugo and Juliette say vous. See the table: Grammar tables, Imparfait: how things were, what used to happen.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Qui ne tente rien n'a rien. »** (kee nuh tahNt ryaN nah ryaN)

*Literally:* Who tries nothing has nothing.

*Meaning:* If you never try, you never get anything.

*English equivalent:* Nothing ventured, nothing gained.

### Episode 15 · Le portrait (The portrait)

*On a Thursday in July, at half past five, the Montmartre café is almost closing. Karim, a portrait painter from the place du Tertre, sits at a table with his box of pencils closed. Rose puts the white cup on her side of the counter and looks at him over her glasses. While he draws her, Socrate sits perfectly still on her shoulder, posing like a statue.*

**Rose:** Bonjour, monsieur. On ferme bientôt.
> *Hello. We're closing soon.* (neutral)

**Karim:** Un thé, s'il vous plaît. Sans question.
> *A tea, please. No question.* (sad)

**Rose:** Sans question, sans thé.
> *No question, no tea.* (teasing)

**Karim:** Je peins dix touristes par jour. Je ne veux plus peindre.
> *I paint ten tourists a day. I don't want to paint any more. (US: anymore)* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Quand vous aviez dix ans, qui est-ce que vous dessiniez ?
> *When you were ten, who did you draw?* (curious)

**Karim:** Ma grand-mère. Je la dessinais tous les dimanches. Elle riait.
> *My grandmother. I drew her every Sunday. She used to laugh.* (moved)

**Rose:** Il faut commencer. Dessinez-moi.
> *You have to start. Draw me.* (hopeful)

**Karim:** Maintenant ? Ici ?
> *Now? Here?* (worried)

**Rose:** Pas mes rides, s'il vous plaît.
> *Not my wrinkles, please.* (amused)

**Rose:** Avant, je courais tout le temps. Une dame m'a arrêtée.
> *Before, I ran all the time. A lady stopped me.* (neutral)

**Karim:** Socrate ne bouge pas ! Et moi, j'ai envie de dessiner encore.
> *Socrate isn't moving! And I feel like drawing more.* (amused)

**Rose:** C'est pour moi ?
> *Is it for me?* (moved)

**Karim:** Oui. Je vous le donne. Ça me fait plaisir.
> *Yes. I'm giving it to you. It's my pleasure.* (proud)

#### Words from this episode

- **Je ne veux plus peindre** (zhuh nuh vuh plew paN-druh) — I don't want to paint any more (ne… plus)
- **dix touristes** (dee too-reest) — ten tourists (dix before a consonant: the x is silent)
- **Quand vous aviez dix ans** (kahN voo‿zah-vyay dee‿zahN) — When you were ten (avoir for age, imparfait)
- **Je la dessinais** (zhuh lah deh-see-neh) — I used to draw her (la = her, before the verb)
- **Elle riait** (el ree-yeh) — She used to laugh (rire: imparfait)
- **Il faut commencer** (eel foh koh-mahN-say) — You have to start (il faut + infinitive)
- **je courais tout le temps** (zhuh koo-reh too luh tahN) — I used to run all the time (courir: imparfait)
- **j'ai envie de dessiner** (zhay ahN-vee duh deh-see-nay) — I feel like drawing (avoir envie de + infinitive)
- **Je vous le donne** (zhuh voo luh dun) — I'm giving it to you (le: it; vous: to you)
- **Ça me fait plaisir** (sah muh feh pleh-zeer) — It makes me happy / It's my pleasure

#### Notice: Object pronouns: je la dessinais, je vous le donne

Karim says Je la dessinais tous les dimanches: la replaces ma grand-mère and goes before the verb. Rose's Dessinez-moi is a command, so the pronoun goes after the verb and me becomes moi. In Je vous le donne, le (the drawing) is the direct object and vous is indirect, because you give something to someone (donner quelque chose à quelqu'un). See the table: Grammar tables, Direct object pronouns: me, le, la...

#### Sagesse du jour

**« L'appétit vient en mangeant. »** (lah-pay-tee vyaN ahN mahN-zhahN)

*Literally:* Appetite comes while eating.

*Meaning:* Once you start doing something, the desire to do it grows.

## Act 4 · Les réponses (The answers)

*Level B1*

### Episode 16 · Cent euros (A hundred euros)

*On a Thursday in September Frédéric, in a perfect coat, walks into Madame Rose's tiny Montmartre café and puts a hundred-euro note on the counter: he has heard about the rule and would like to skip it. Socrate the grey parrot hops down from his perch and nibbles one corner of the note. Rose pulls the white cup back to her side of the counter and looks at him over her glasses.*

**Frédéric:** Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais un café. Sans la question. Voilà cent euros.
> *Hello. I'd like a coffee. Without the question. Here's a hundred euros.* (proud)

**Rose:** Vous avez de la monnaie ? Le café coûte deux euros. La question est gratuite.
> *Have you got any change? The coffee costs two euros. The question is free.* (teasing)

**Frédéric:** Alors, j'achète l'ardoise. Ou le perroquet, même s'il coûte les yeux de la tête !
> *Then I'll buy the slate. Or the parrot, even if it costs an arm and a leg! (literally: the eyes of the head)* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Regardez Socrate. Il mange le coin de votre billet !
> *Look at Socrate. He's eating the corner of your note! (US: bill)* (amused)

**Rose:** Qui est-ce que vous aimeriez appeler ce soir ?
> *Who would you like to call tonight?* (curious)

**Frédéric:** Personne… Personne ne m'appelle. Mon téléphone ne sonne jamais.
> *Nobody… Nobody calls me. My phone never rings.* (sad)

**Frédéric:** Mon frère, Marc, habite à Lyon. On ne s'appelle plus depuis dix ans.
> *My brother, Marc, lives in Lyon. We haven't phoned each other for ten years.* (sad)

**Frédéric:** Une histoire d'argent. La maison de nos parents. C'est bête.
> *It was about money. Our parents' house. It's silly.* (annoyed)

**Rose:** Le plus beau cadeau de ma vie ? C'était une question.
> *The best present of my life? It was a question. (US: gift)* (moved)

**Frédéric:** Je voudrais l'appeler. J'aimerais lui dire pardon.
> *I'd like to call him. I'd like to say sorry to him.* (hopeful)

**Rose:** On pourrait commencer par un café, non ?
> *We could start with a coffee, couldn't we?* (teasing)

**Frédéric:** Merci, madame. Je paie : deux euros. Et… mon billet ?
> *Thank you. I'm paying: two euros. And… my note? (US: bill)* (relieved)

**Rose:** Reprenez votre billet. Il n'est pas à vendre, mon perroquet.
> *Take your note back. My parrot is not for sale. (US: bill)* (amused)

#### Words from this episode

- **Je voudrais un café** (zhuh voo-dreh uhN kah-fay) — I'd like a coffee (polite)
- **cent euros** (sahN‿tuh-roh) — a hundred euros (t liaison: cent euros)
- **j'achète l'ardoise** (zhah-shet lar-dwahz) — I'll buy the slate (acheter: j'achète)
- **coûte les yeux de la tête** (koot lay‿zyuh duh lah tet) — costs an arm and a leg (literally: the eyes of the head)
- **Qui est-ce que vous aimeriez appeler** (kee es-kuh voo‿zeh-muh-ryay ah-puh-lay) — Who would you like to call (a wish: conditional)
- **Personne ne m'appelle** (pair-sun nuh mah-pel) — Nobody calls me (appeler: two l before a silent e)
- **Je voudrais l'appeler** (zhuh voo-dreh lah-puh-lay) — I'd like to call him (vouloir, polite)
- **J'aimerais lui dire pardon** (zhem-reh lwee deer par-dohN) — I'd like to say sorry to him (aimer, a wish)
- **On pourrait commencer** (ohN poo-reh koh-mahN-say) — We could start (pouvoir, a soft suggestion)
- **Je paie** (zhuh peh) — I'm paying (payer)

#### Notice: Polite and wishing forms: je voudrais, j'aimerais, on pourrait

Frédéric orders with Je voudrais un café and later says J'aimerais lui dire pardon. Rose asks Qui est-ce que vous aimeriez appeler ? and suggests On pourrait commencer par un café. These conditional forms soften a request, state a wish or make a gentle suggestion; Je veux un café is much blunter. See the table: Grammar tables, Conditional: would, could, polite requests.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« L'argent ne fait pas le bonheur. »** (lar-zhahN nuh feh pah luh bu-nuhr)

*Literally:* Money doesn't make happiness.

*Meaning:* Being rich doesn't make you happy.

*English equivalent:* Money can't buy happiness.

### Episode 17 · Tel père… (Like father…)

*On a Friday in September Paul, the groom from March, comes back to Madame Rose's tiny Montmartre café. He is holding a small black-and-white scan picture: his wife Léa is expecting a baby in December. Rose puts the white cup on her side of the counter, and Socrate watches from his perch by the window.*

**Paul:** Bonjour, madame Rose ! Vous vous souvenez de moi ? Le discours de trois phrases !
> *Hello, Madame Rose! Do you remember me? The three-sentence speech!* (proud)

**Rose:** Bien sûr ! Le discours le plus court de Paris. Et Léa, ça va ?
> *Of course! The shortest speech in Paris. And how's Léa?* (amused)

**Paul:** Très bien. Regardez cette photo… Léa attend un bébé. Il va naître en décembre !
> *Very well. Look at this picture… Léa's expecting a baby. It's due in December!* (proud)

**Rose:** Un bébé ! C'est génial ! Félicitations, monsieur Paul !
> *A baby! That's brilliant! Congratulations, Paul!* (surprised)

**Paul:** Merci. Mais j'ai peur. Mon père n'était jamais là. Il travaillait tout le temps.
> *Thank you. But I'm scared. My father was never there. He worked all the time.* (worried)

**Paul:** Tel père, tel fils, non ?
> *Like father, like son, right?* (sad)

**Rose:** Quel père est-ce que vous aimeriez être ?
> *What kind of father would you like to be?* (curious)

**Paul:** Le père que je voudrais être ? Un père qui est là.
> *The father I'd like to be? A father who's there.* (hopeful)

**Paul:** Qui joue. Qui pose des questions.
> *Who plays. Who asks questions.* (hopeful)

**Rose:** Mon père voulait une avocate. Il a eu une patronne de café.
> *My father wanted a lawyer for a daughter. He got a café owner.* (amused)

**Rose:** Mais il venait chaque dimanche pour la tarte.
> *But he came every Sunday for the tart.* (moved)

**Rose:** Alors, tel père, tel fils… c'est vous qui choisissez le père.
> *So, like father, like son… but you're the one who chooses the father.* (hopeful)

**Paul:** J'aimerais l'appeler Rose… si c'est une fille.
> *I'd like to call her Rose… if it's a girl.* (moved)

**Rose:** Regardez Socrate, il vous tourne le dos ! Socrate voudrait Socrate.
> *Look at Socrate, he's turning his back on you! Socrate would rather it was called Socrate.* (amused)

#### Words from this episode

- **Vous vous souvenez de moi** (voo voo soo-vuh-nay duh mwah) — Do you remember me? (se souvenir de)
- **Il va naître** (eel vah neh-truh) — It's going to be born (naître, near future)
- **en décembre** (ahN day-sahN-bruh) — in December (en + month)
- **C'est génial** (seh zhay-nyahl) — That's brilliant
- **Il travaillait tout le temps** (eel trah-vah-yeh too luh tahN) — He worked all the time (imparfait: a habit)
- **Quel père est-ce que vous aimeriez être** (kel pair es-kuh voo‿zeh-muh-ryay eh-truh) — What kind of father would you like to be (a wish)
- **Le père que je voudrais être** (luh pair kuh zhuh voo-dreh eh-truh) — The father I'd like to be (que: not the subject)
- **Un père qui est là** (uhN pair kee eh lah) — A father who's there (qui: the subject)
- **c'est vous qui choisissez** (seh voo kee shwah-zee-say) — you're the one who chooses (choisir)

#### Notice: Qui and que: un père qui est là

Paul says Le père que je voudrais être ? Un père qui est là. Qui is the subject of its clause (the father is there), so a verb follows it directly; que is used when the clause already has its own subject, here je. Rose uses qui too: c'est vous qui choisissez le père. See the table: Grammar tables, Relative pronouns: qui, que, où, dont.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Tel père, tel fils. »** (tel pair, tel fees)

*Literally:* Such father, such son.

*Meaning:* Children often grow up like their parents.

*English equivalent:* Like father, like son.

---

### Episode 18 · L'histoire de Rose (Rose's story)

*On Friday at six, closing time, the chairs are up on the three little tables of Madame Rose's Montmartre café. Hugo, her great-nephew, has taken down the postcards to dust them: forty cards of the sea, all signed O. Rose sits down with her blue cup, and Socrate sleeps on the counter.*

**Hugo:** Quarante cartes, Tata. Et toujours la même question ?
> *Forty cards, Auntie. And always the same question?* (curious)

**Rose:** Ici, c'est moi qui pose les questions.
> *Here, I'm the one who asks the questions.* (teasing)

**Hugo:** Il n'y a pas de clients. C'est fermé.
> *There are no customers. We're closed.* (teasing)

**Rose:** Bon. Assieds-toi. Tu sais pourquoi j'ai gardé cette règle ?
> *Right. Sit down. Do you know why I kept this rule?* (curious)

**Hugo:** Non. Tu n'en dis jamais rien.
> *No. You never say anything about it.* (curious)

**Rose:** À vingt-deux ans, j'étais étudiante en droit. Je courais partout.
> *At twenty-two, I was a law student. I ran everywhere.* (neutral)

**Rose:** Un matin, Odette m'a demandé : « Pourquoi vous courez ? »
> *One morning, Odette asked me: 'Why are you running?'* (moved)

**Rose:** Je lui ai répondu : « Parce que je suis en retard. » — « En retard pour quoi ? »
> *I answered: 'Because I'm late.' And she said: 'Late for what?'* (amused)

**Rose:** Je n'avais pas de réponse. Je me suis assise. Je suis restée une heure.
> *I had no answer. I sat down. I stayed an hour.* (moved)

**Rose:** J'ai quitté le droit. En quatre-vingt-six, elle m'a laissé le café, la tarte et Socrate.
> *I gave up law. In '86 she left me the café, the tart and Socrate.* (proud)

**Rose:** « Il aime le café, pas la mer. » Rien ne sert de courir… tu connais la suite ?
> *'He loves the café, not the sea,' she said. There's no point running… do you know the rest?* (amused)

**Hugo:** Il faut partir à point. Mais pourquoi tu n'y es jamais allée, à Saint-Malo ?
> *You have to set off at the right time. But why have you never been there, to Saint-Malo?* (curious)

**Rose:** Je… Le café ne peut pas attendre.
> *I… The café can't wait.* (surprised)

**Hugo:** Un café, ça réveille. Une question, ça réveille plus.
> *A coffee wakes you up. A question wakes you up more.* (proud)

#### Words from this episode

- **Tu n'en dis jamais rien** (tew nahN dee zhah-meh ryaN) — You never say anything about it (en = about it)
- **j'étais étudiante en droit** (zhay-teh ay-tew-dyahNt ahN drwah) — I was a law student (imparfait: description)
- **Je courais partout** (zhuh koo-reh par-too) — I ran everywhere (courir, imparfait: a habit)
- **Parce que je suis en retard** (pars kuh zhuh swee‿zahN ruh-tar) — Because I'm late
- **Je me suis assise** (zhuh muh swee ah-seez) — I sat down (s'asseoir; assise: Rose is a woman)
- **Je suis restée une heure** (zhuh swee res-tay ewn uhr) — I stayed an hour (rester takes être)
- **J'ai quitté le droit** (zhay kee-tay luh drwah) — I gave up law (quitter: to leave a place, a job, studies)
- **elle m'a laissé le café** (el mah leh-say luh kah-fay) — she left me the café (laisser: to leave something to someone)
- **tu n'y es jamais allée** (tew nee eh zhah-meh ah-lay) — you've never been there (y = to Saint-Malo)

#### Notice: En and y: tu n'en dis rien, tu n'y es jamais allée

Hugo says Tu n'en dis jamais rien: en stands for 'about it' (de cette histoire). Then he asks Pourquoi tu n'y es jamais allée, à Saint-Malo ?: y stands for 'there' (à Saint-Malo), and both go before the verb. Notice too that in 1978 Odette said vous to Rose (Pourquoi vous courez ?), a customer she didn't know yet; today her cards say tu. See the table: Grammar tables, Y and en.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Rien ne sert de courir ; il faut partir à point. »** (ryaN nuh sair duh koo-reer, eel foh par-teer ah pwaN)

*Literally:* Running is no use; you must set off at the right time.

*Meaning:* Rushing doesn't help; start calmly, at the right moment.

*English equivalent:* Slow and steady wins the race.

### Episode 19 · Pourquoi tu cours ? (Why are you running?)

*On Saturday at a quarter past eight Hugo runs into the café with a law textbook under his arm: he revised all night for Monday's exam. Madame Rose is waiting at the counter with her blue cup and a white one. She pours his coffee and keeps it on her side. Later she takes a card from the drawer under the till.*

**Rose:** Huit heures et quart, mon grand.
> *A quarter past eight, my boy.* (teasing)

**Hugo:** J'arrive ! Pardon, Tata ! Je suis en retard !
> *Coming! Sorry, Auntie! I'm late!* (worried)

**Rose:** Pourquoi tu cours ?
> *Why are you running?* (curious)

**Hugo:** Parce que je suis en retard.
> *Because I'm late.* (neutral)

**Rose:** En retard pour quoi ?
> *Late for what?* (neutral)

**Hugo:** Parce que… le droit, c'est bien ?
> *Because… law is good?* (amused)

**Rose:** Regarde Socrate. Il te tourne le dos.
> *Look at Socrate. He's turning his back on you.* (teasing)

**Hugo:** Attends… Tu m'as posé la question d'Odette.
> *Wait… You've just asked me Odette's question.* (surprised)

**Hugo:** J'aimerais être pâtissier. Je voudrais faire un CAP. Mais mes parents…
> *I'd like to be a pastry chef. I'd like to do a CAP (a vocational diploma). But my parents…* (sad)

**Rose:** C'est ta vie, mon grand. Et c'est une bonne idée.
> *It's your life, my boy. And it's a good idea.* (hopeful)

**Hugo:** Tu as raison. Je vais le dire à mes parents. Ce soir.
> *You're right. I'm going to tell my parents. Tonight.* (proud)

**Rose:** Voilà la recette d'Odette. Elle est à toi, maintenant.
> *Here's Odette's recipe. It's yours now.* (moved)

**Hugo:** Merci, Tata. Et… mon café ?
> *Thanks, Auntie. And… my coffee?* (amused)

#### Words from this episode

- **Huit heures et quart** (wee‿tuhr ay kar) — A quarter past eight (t liaison after huit; none after et)
- **J'arrive** (zhah-reev) — Coming! / I'm on my way
- **Je suis en retard** (zhuh swee‿zahN ruh-tar) — I'm late
- **Pourquoi tu cours** (poor-kwah tew koor) — Why are you running? (courir: tu cours)
- **J'aimerais être pâtissier** (zhem-reh eh-truh pah-tee-syay) — I'd like to be a pastry chef (a wish; no article before the job)
- **Je voudrais faire un CAP** (zhuh voo-dreh fair uhN say-ah-pay) — I'd like to do a CAP (a vocational diploma)
- **C'est ta vie** (seh tah vee) — It's your life (c'est + ta + noun)
- **Je vais le dire à mes parents** (zhuh veh luh deer ah may pah-rahN) — I'm going to tell my parents (dire, near future)
- **Elle est à toi** (el eh ah twah) — It's yours (à toi: stressed pronoun)

#### Notice: C'est ta vie, but il est pâtissier

Rose says C'est ta vie and C'est une bonne idée: c'est comes before a determiner (ta, une) and a noun. For a job after être, French uses no article: Hugo says J'aimerais être pâtissier, and you say Il est pâtissier or Il est étudiant. See the table: Grammar tables, C'est or il est?

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Vouloir, c'est pouvoir. »** (voo-lwahr, seh poo-vwahr)

*Literally:* To want is to be able.

*Meaning:* If you really want something, you find a way.

*English equivalent:* Where there's a will, there's a way.

---

### Episode 20 · La question pour Rose (The question for Rose)

*On Saturday 17 October Thomas, the man in a hurry from the first episode, walks slowly into Madame Rose's Montmartre café, with no phone. Hugo, silent behind the counter, has told him Rose's story, and Thomas pushes the white cup across to Rose's side. When Thomas says that Socrate likes travelling, the grey parrot whistles for the first time in years: his yes to Saint-Malo. At the end Rose picks up the chalk and writes two sentences on the slate, under Odette's rule.*

**Thomas:** Bonjour, madame Rose. Aujourd'hui, c'est moi qui pose la question.
> *Good morning, Madame Rose. Today, I'm the one asking the question.* (proud)

**Rose:** Ici, c'est moi qui pose les questions.
> *Here, I'm the one who asks the questions.* (teasing)

**Thomas:** Pas aujourd'hui.
> *Not today.* (teasing)

**Rose:** Vous marchez, maintenant ?
> *So you walk now?* (teasing)

**Thomas:** Je marche. Chaque chose en son temps. Et vous, madame Rose, qu'est-ce que vous aimeriez ?
> *I walk. All in good time. And you, Madame Rose, what would you like?* (curious)

**Rose:** Moi ? Personne ne me pose jamais la question.
> *Me? Nobody ever asks me that.* (surprised)

**Rose:** J'aimerais revoir Odette. Lui dire merci. Et voir la mer.
> *I'd like to see Odette again. To say thank you. And to see the sea.* (moved)

**Thomas:** Saint-Malo, c'est à deux heures et demie de train.
> *Saint-Malo is two and a half hours by train.* (neutral)

**Rose:** Et le café ? Et Socrate ?
> *And the café? And Socrate?* (worried)

**Thomas:** Hugo est là. Et Socrate aime les voyages, non ?
> *Hugo's here. And Socrate likes travelling, doesn't he? (US: traveling)* (amused)

**Rose:** Il a sifflé ! Il ne siffle jamais !
> *He whistled! He never whistles!* (surprised)

**Rose:** On pourrait partir lundi… À quelle heure part le train ?
> *We could leave on Monday… What time does the train leave?* (hopeful)

**Thomas:** À huit heures.
> *At eight o'clock.* (neutral)

**Rose:** Lundi, c'est Hugo. Je vais répondre à une question. Votre café. Aujourd'hui, sans question.
> *On Monday, Hugo's in charge. I'm going to answer a question. Your coffee. Today, no question.* (amused)

#### Words from this episode

- **c'est moi qui pose la question** (seh mwah kee pohz lah kes-tyohN) — I'm the one asking the question (poser une question)
- **Vous marchez** (voo mar-shay) — You walk (marcher)
- **qu'est-ce que vous aimeriez** (kes-kuh voo‿zeh-muh-ryay) — what would you like (a wish: conditional)
- **J'aimerais revoir Odette** (zhem-reh ruh-vwahr oh-det) — I'd like to see Odette again (aimer, a wish)
- **voir la mer** (vwahr lah mair) — to see the sea (voir)
- **deux heures et demie** (duh‿zuhr ay duh-mee) — two and a half hours (z liaison after deux)
- **On pourrait partir lundi** (ohN poo-reh par-teer luhN-dee) — We could leave on Monday (a soft suggestion)
- **À quelle heure part le train** (ah kel uhr par luh traN) — What time does the train leave?
- **À quelle heure** (ah kel uhr) — At what time (quelle: heure is feminine)

#### Notice: Wishing: vous aimeriez, j'aimerais, on pourrait

Thomas asks Qu'est-ce que vous aimeriez ? and Rose answers J'aimerais revoir Odette. Aimer in the conditional states a wish, and On pourrait partir lundi… makes a soft suggestion. Compare the present J'aime la mer: a fact, not a wish. See the table: Grammar tables, Conditional: would, could, polite requests.

#### Sagesse du jour

**« Tout est bien qui finit bien. »** (too‿teh byaN kee fee-nee byaN)

*Literally:* All is well that ends well.

*Meaning:* A happy ending makes the difficulties worth it.

*English equivalent:* All's well that ends well.

## Proverb index

- Episode 1 · « Chaque chose en son temps. » — Give each thing its own moment: finish your coffee before the next task.
- Episode 2 · « Il ne faut pas chercher midi à quatorze heures. » — Don't make a simple thing complicated.
- Episode 3 · « Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid. » — Patience and small steps get big things done.
- Episode 4 · « Paris ne s'est pas fait en un jour. » — Great things take time and patience; you can't do them all at once.
- Episode 5 · « Qui ne dit mot consent. » — If you say nothing, people think you agree.
- Episode 6 · « C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron. » — You learn by doing it again and again, mistakes included.
- Episode 7 · « Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or. » — Things that look wonderful aren't always what they seem.
- Episode 8 · « Il n'y a pas de sot métier. » — Every honest job deserves respect; none is beneath anyone.
- Episode 9 · « Mieux vaut tard que jamais. » — It's better to do something late than not at all.
- Episode 10 · « Il n'est pire sourd que celui qui ne veut pas entendre. » — The hardest person to reach is the one who won't listen.
- Episode 11 · « C'est dans les vieux pots qu'on fait les meilleures soupes. » — Experience and age are an advantage, not a weakness.
- Episode 12 · « Le mieux est l'ennemi du bien. » — Trying to make something perfect can spoil what was already good.
- Episode 13 · « La vérité sort de la bouche des enfants. » — Children often say simple true things that adults avoid.
- Episode 14 · « Qui ne tente rien n'a rien. » — If you never try, you never get anything.
- Episode 15 · « L'appétit vient en mangeant. » — Once you start doing something, the desire to do it grows.
- Episode 16 · « L'argent ne fait pas le bonheur. » — Being rich doesn't make you happy.
- Episode 17 · « Tel père, tel fils. » — Children often grow up like their parents.
- Episode 18 · « Rien ne sert de courir ; il faut partir à point. » — Rushing doesn't help; start calmly, at the right moment.
- Episode 19 · « Vouloir, c'est pouvoir. » — If you really want something, you find a way.
- Episode 20 · « Tout est bien qui finit bien. » — A happy ending makes the difficulties worth it.
